content.title: Related Work
content.comment:
Hi authors, I really like your work on using gradient norm regularizers to improve generalization. Please consider citing the following paper that also utilizes the eigenvalues of the Hessian for better generalization.

[1] Information-Theoretic Local Minima Characterization and Regularization

ICML 2020

Zhiwei Jia, Hao Su

content.summary_of_the_paper: The author proposed a new regularization method, named Gradient Norm Regularizer (GNR), to help deep neural networks to find more flat local minima. The experiment results show that GNR can improve the generalization performance of different types of DNNs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. A new method to help DNNs to find local minima.
2.  Theoretical analysis and understanding of the proposed GNR are complete and comprehensive.
3.  An practical implementation for GNR is proposed.

Weaknesses:
1. The implementation of GNR uses the Hessian vector product, which may consume a lot of computation and memory.
2. The experiments seem only conducted on image classification tasks.
3. The baseline of ResNet50 on ImageNet is too low.
4. The comparison of memory consumption is not given.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the proposed method is clear,  the quality of the work is solid, originality of the work is sufficient.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The proposed method Gradient Norm Regularizer (GNR) is a novel method to improve the generalization performance of DNNs, and the author provides a practical way to implement GNR in training DNNs. But it needs more additional computation and memory consumption. 
More experiments beyond image classification tasks in the experiment part would make GNR more convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights as a regularization technique
that targets flat minima. For small radius rho the regularization corresponds to minimizing the maximum eigenvalue of the hessian. 
In standard computer vision benchmarks, they show better accuracy when used with SGD variants and also when combined with
SAM, another flat minima-seeking algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well written, the results interesting, and I appreciated both the theoretical analysis and the
experiments. 
Nonetheless,  in my opinion the proposed regularization doesn't improve over more convenient alternatives. Also, the regularization has already been proposed in the past.

My major concerns are the following:

- The gradient regularization technique has already been proposed in Barret and Dehrin ICLR 2021 (section 4, explicit gradient regularization). Since it wasn't the main focus of the paper it was not thoroughly tested but it is nonetheless linked to good generalization
and flat minima. The authors of the present manuscript didn't cite that paper.

- The GNR regularization seems to be equivalent for small rho to the surrogate gap regularization of GSAM (Zhuang et al ICLR '22).
  GSAM is a simpler algorithm compared to GNR and seems to yield the same (if not better) results.
  
- The benefits of GNR are very small when applied on top of SAM and don't seem worth the additional complexity.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear and well written. Results are not entirely original.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Another nice attempt at devising an algorithm targeting flat minima, but I don't think it passes
the ICLR bar since it doesn't seem to improve over the many alternatives available and since the same regularization 
has already been proposed in the past.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a regularisation objective for supervised learning, that tries to simulaneously minimize the empirical loss and a term that captures a notion of "flatness" through the norm of the gradient of the loss function (with respect to the parameters of the network). This notion of flatness is stronger than the one presented in the original SAM paper (Foret et al 2021) but it is not argued why is it a better notion. A heuristic algorithm that tries to optimize the objective by doing multiple approximations is presented. An analysis of its convergence to first-order stationarity is presented but one which has multiple flaws. In practical experiments the algorithm is shown to enjoy a marginal improvement over the baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. Paper does not cite https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/zhao22i/zhao22i.pdf which is almost the same idea. Hence, the novelty is questionable and in any case the authors should have cited this work and compared the methods.
2. Proposition 2.1 which is stated as one of the main contributions is straightforward. The authors use the assumption that the loss "can be second-order Taylor-approximated in a neighborhood of a local minimum $\theta^*$", but in fact they simply assume the loss function is equal to a quadratic i.e. $L(\theta)=\frac{1}{2} \theta^\top A \theta$ (without loss of generality we can assume $\theta^*=0$). From this it is trivial that $\nabla L(\theta) = A\theta$ so that $\max_{\|\theta\| \leq \rho} \nabla L(\theta) = \max_{\|\theta\| \leq \rho} \| A \theta \|$ which is the well-known operator norm of $A$, which is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix (also well known). From this well-known facts their result follows. I do not believe this can be claimed as a contribution. In particular, the proof provided in the appendix is much more complicated than necessary.
3. The paper claims that some methods fail to measure flatness/sharpness and that GNR does not. However, the authors never present what is the formal definition of flatness that they refer to. Truth is, there is no "correct" definition of "flatness", instead one can define flatness using some order of derivatives. For example, the notion of flatness that the original SAM optimizes is the zero-th order flatness defined as the maximum change of the function over a region. The notion of flatness proposed by the authors is the "first-order flatness" defined as a the maximum norm of the gradient over a region. As the authors observe, their notion of flatness is stronger than the 0-th order flatness, as having a small gradient leads to a bound on the value of the function. However, one can have a function that is flat (in the zero-th order sense) but that is not even differentiable or has arbitrarily large value of the derivative!
4. For example, in the paragraph in page 2, following Definition 2.1 it is stated that "when L is flat it should not change drastically in the neighborhood of $\theta$" this is simply not true if the definition of flatness is the least restrictive (the zero-th order flatness)
5. The same can be extended to higher orders, we could demand an even stronger notion of flatness that requires a small value of the norm of the Hessian over a ball and derive analogous methods of regularization of higher order derivatives.
6. In summary, the authors use the notion of flatness that is more convenient to them, and it is never defined formally. This makes claims like the one in the caption of Figure 1: "GNR can distinguish flatness while SAM could not" simply misleading. Authors should simply state that their method tries to regularize a stronger notion of flatness than that of SAM. It is not clear or at least it is not argued by the authors why one notion of flatness is better/worse than the other.
7. Theorem 2.3 does not present any rigorous result. Note that the result is some sort of expected first-order stationarity of a function $L^{\text{overall}}$ which is defined in equation (4). The problem is that definition (4) includes the parameter $\rho$ which is the perturbation radius and should be assumed to be a fixed value, but in the algorithm the value of $\rho$ is actually varying per iteration (it is instead denoted by $\rho_t$) and tends to zero! So what is the point? For which $\rho$ in $L^{\text{overall}}$ is Theorem 2.3 obtaining first-order stationarity?
8. In fact, it makes no sense to talk about the expected norm of the gradient of $L^{\text{overall}}$ because the regularizer is not differentiable.
9. The experiments section is the strongest part of the paper, but it is eclipsed by the weak sections preceding it.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Originality: can be questioned as the Paper does not cite https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/zhao22i/zhao22i.pdf which is almost the same idea. Also the same idea has been explored in adversarial training, instead regularizing the gradient with respect to the input of the model.
2. Clarity: The formal notion of "flatness" that the authors refer to is never defined, so their claims are not clear. The convergence result Theorem 2.3 is not clear what tries to achieve, the notation is not good as the function that is supposedly minimized has a fixed hyperparameter, that instead changes during the iterations of the algorithm
3. Quality: The statements regarding optimization do not show domain of the topic. Proposition 2.1 is straightforward and its proof much more complicated than needed. The quality of the experiments is good though.
4. Reproducibility: As far as I see, the authors didn't provide any code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Experiments show that the method might be promising, but the theoretical section is riddled with issues and flaws. Authors are better off removing or vastly improving the theoretical section. The paper needs major rewriting. More importantly, they need to compare to the highly similar method from https://proceedings.mlr.press/v162/zhao22i/zhao22i.pdf which as far as I know, appeared well in advance of the deadline for this conference. I cannot recommend acceptance currently.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a gradient norm regularizer (GNR) to guide optimizers to find flatter minima that generalize better. They attempt to argue that GNR can resolve the issue of SAM when encountering multiple minima around convergent solutions. As a result, they claim that GNR performs better than SAM and empirical experiments (on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet) are also provided
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strong point 
The phenomenon pointed out in Figure 1 seems quite interesting. It basically says that when the radius $\rho$ is large, it is very possible that the surrogate flatness in SAM can be a very bad measurement of the true flatness. In particular, this happens when there are multiple minima around the convergent one. 

The experiment results seem to suggest that the proposed GNR regularization is orthogonal to SAM. It seems that combining SAM with GNR  consistently performs better than vanilla SAM.

### Weak point

 **The motivation does not make too much sense to me**. 
In deep learning, usually, all global minima are connected instead of isolated, which is quite different from the picture illustrated in Figure 1. The experiment in Section 3.1 suggests that there are several minimum valleys with the radius, which might be relevant. However, I find the experiment description quite confusing. For instance, what does it mean by "we repeatedly add a perturbation with the norm of 0.01 along the direction 10 times"? If the direction is fixed, then how can you repeat adding different perturbations? In addition, I would like to see visualizations of the landscape along these directions instead of only reporting the ``frequency'' of finding local minima, where the result I find suspicious. 


A more serious issue is that the accuracies reported do not show that GNR can consistently perform better than SAM. In fact, as far as I can tell, the test performance is degraded in most cases.  For instance, in Table 2 (ResNet 50 on ImageNet), GNR consistently performs worse than SAM. The experiment results seem to suggest that the combination of GNR and SAM outperforms vanilla SAM, but this improvement is never explained and analyzed.

Lastly, I feel there are lots of writing/exposition issues with this submission. 

- In tables, the authors bolded their results (the ones using GNR) instead of the best ones. This is very misleading. 

- The experimental setup and description are also confusing. For instance, when reporting the GNR result, the base optimizer is stated but it is unclear what is the base optimizer for SAM. 

- I think Proposition 2.2 has nothing related to the proposed method. I am aware that many people attempt to prove some (fake) theorems to make their empirical observations look more solid. But this is not necessary and even a waste of time to readers.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is clear but kind of misleading.  It is unclear if the proposed method outperforms the baseline.
content.summary_of_the_review: In a summary, this submission perhaps contains some interesting findings. However, according to the explanation above, I feel that this work is still preliminary at this stage and needs more investigation.

content.title: Gradient Norm Regularizer Seeks Flat Minima and Improves Generalization
content.abstract: The heavy overparameterization of current deep neural networks requires model generalization guarantees. Recently, flat minima are proven to be effective for improving generalization and sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) achieves state-of-the-art performance. Yet we show that SAM fails to measure flatness/sharpness when there are multiple minima within the perturbation radius. We present a novel regularizer named Gradient Norm Regularizer (GNR) to seek minima with uniformly small curvature across all directions and measure sharpness even when multiple minima are within the perturbation radius. We show that GNR bounds both the maximum eigenvalue of Hessian at local minima and the regularization function of SAM. We present experimental results showing that GNR improves the generalization of models trained with current optimizers such as SGD and AdamW on various datasets and networks. Furthermore, we show that GNR can help SAM find flatter minima and achieve better generalization.
